title: Symmetric Lab — Build a Mini libsodium

questions.question: What does libsodium's `crypto_secretbox_easy` return?
options: Only the ciphertext — the caller stores the nonce separately
The MAC tag alone — encryption is done by a separate call
A combined blob containing nonce, authentication tag, and ciphertext
Only the nonce — the caller must XOR it with the plaintext
questions.explanation: secretbox_easy returns a self-contained blob: nonce (or MAC) prepended to ciphertext, so the receiver needs only this one value to decrypt and verify.

questions.question: Why is HKDF not a suitable replacement for PBKDF2 when hashing passwords?
options: HKDF uses SHA-256 which is too weak for passwords
HKDF is designed to be fast; password KDFs must be slow to deter guessing
HKDF does not accept a salt parameter
HKDF output length is fixed at 32 bytes
questions.explanation: HKDF is designed for speed — it expands high-entropy keys quickly. Password KDFs (PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2) are deliberately slow so that offline guessing attacks are expensive. Using HKDF on a password gives attackers a fast offline oracle.

questions.question: In the mini-libsodium secretbox, what is the format of the returned `box` blob?
options: ciphertext || tag (nonce stored separately)
tag || ciphertext (nonce stored separately)
nonce || tag || ciphertext (self-contained)
nonce || ciphertext (tag implicit)
questions.explanation: The box is nonce (12 bytes) || tag (16 bytes) || ciphertext. Prepending the nonce makes the blob self-contained — the receiver extracts all three fields without needing a separate channel for the nonce.

questions.question: In `kdf_derive_from_key(subkey_len, subkey_id, ctx, key)`, what is the role of `ctx`?
options: It is the salt fed into HKDF Extract, randomizing the PRK
It labels the domain so different application modules derive independent subkeys even with the same master key and subkey_id
It sets the output length of the derived subkey
It is the counter that ensures each call produces a different key
questions.explanation: The `ctx` (context) is a domain-separation label. Two modules using different `ctx` values with the same master key and subkey_id will derive completely unrelated subkeys. It is encoded into HKDF's `info` field alongside the subkey_id.

questions.question: In `secretstream`, how does the receiver detect a replayed chunk?
options: It checks a sequence number field embedded in each chunk
The nonce is nonce_base || counter; a replayed chunk has the wrong counter and fails Poly1305 authentication
Each chunk includes a timestamp that the receiver validates
The receiver maintains a list of all chunk hashes and rejects duplicates
questions.explanation: Each chunk's 12-byte nonce is nonce_base (8 B) || counter (4 B). A replayed chunk encrypted at counter i will be decrypted with counter j ≠ i, producing the wrong one-time Poly1305 key and a tag verification failure.

questions.question: Why does `auth_verify` use `hmac.compare_digest` instead of `==`?
options: Because `==` raises TypeError on bytes
To prevent short-circuit evaluation from leaking how many bytes match, which attackers can use to forge tags
Because `hmac.compare_digest` is faster for 32-byte values
To support comparing tags of different lengths without padding
questions.explanation: `==` on bytes exits early as soon as a byte differs, leaking timing information about how many bytes matched. An attacker can exploit this to forge a valid tag one byte at a time. `hmac.compare_digest` always compares all bytes in constant time.

questions.question: What happens if you call `secretstream_push` and `secretstream_pull` with the same key and header but then replay chunk 0 as chunk 2 on the pull side?
options: Pull silently decrypts it because the key is the same
Pull raises ValueError because chunk 0's tag was computed with counter=0, not counter=2
Pull succeeds but returns corrupted plaintext
Pull skips the chunk and continues to chunk 3
questions.explanation: The pull counter is at 2, so it computes a nonce using counter=2. Chunk 0 was encrypted with counter=0, so the Poly1305 one-time key differs, the tag check fails, and ValueError is raised.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a design goal of the mini-libsodium API?
options: Nonce generation is automatic so callers cannot accidentally reuse a nonce
Key separation is enforced by requiring a distinct `ctx` and `subkey_id` per use
The caller chooses the encryption algorithm (AES-GCM or ChaCha20) at runtime
Authentication failures raise an exception rather than returning a sentinel value
questions.explanation: libsodium deliberately hides algorithm choice. The goal is an opinionated API where the algorithm is pre-selected (ChaCha20-Poly1305) and callers cannot accidentally choose a weaker option. Flexibility in algorithm choice is a footgun, not a feature.
